content: Phosphorous acid, chemically represented as H₃PO₃, is one of the oxoacids of phosphorus. Other notable members of this group include phosphoric acid (H₃PO₄) and hypophosphorous acid (H₃PO₂). The naming convention for reduced phosphorus compounds uses the suffix -ous. Alternative names for phosphorous acid include orthophosphorous acid and dihydroxyphosphine oxide. The compound H₃PO₃ is produced through the hydrolysis of its acid anhydride, P₄O₆, in a manner analogous to the relationship between H₃PO₄ and P₄O₁₀. Structurally, H₃PO₃ is better described as HP(O)(OH)₂, which exists in equilibrium with a minor tautomer, P(OH)₃. The latter is also referred to as phosphorous acid and is recognized by its IUPAC name, phosphorous acid, with CAS number 10294-56-1 and CID 107909. The dihydroxy form, HP(O)(OH)₂, is known as phosphonic acid. Many reduced phosphorus acids exhibit complex equilibria involving hydrogen shifts between oxygen and phosphorus atoms. In its solid state, HP(O)(OH)₂ adopts a tetrahedral geometry, featuring one shorter P=O bond (148 pm) and two longer P–O(H) bonds (154 pm). Phosphorous acid is commercially available but is often synthesized by hydrolyzing phosphorus trichloride (PCl₃) with water or steam. Potassium phosphite serves as a convenient precursor for phosphorous acid. In practice, aqueous potassium phosphite is treated with excess hydrochloric acid, and the pure acid is isolated by concentrating the solution and precipitating it with alcohols. Oligophosphorous acids are formed by condensing a few molecules of phosphorous acid, resulting in the loss of water. Polyphosphorous acids, on the other hand, can consist of dozens of condensed units, with each addition involving the loss of H₂O. For both tautomers, the repeating unit is (HPO₂)ₙ₋₂. For example, triphosphosphonic acid and triphosphorous acid both have the formula H₅P₃O₇ when n = 3. In sufficiently large oligophosphorous acids, multiple hydroxyl groups can lead to the formation of cyclophosphorous acids, which do not contain multiple (HPO₃) metaphosphoric acid units. However, the term cyclophosphorous acid may sometimes be a misnomer, as the cyclic portion may be carbon-based with a phosphorous acid side chain or include one or more tautomeric forms as a minority component. The effect of varying ring size on the phosphonate-phosphite tautomerism of cyclophosphorous acids has been demonstrated. Cyclophosphorous acids are typically biheteroorganic, and branching can occur in both oligophosphorous and polyphosphorous tautomers. Phosphorous acid is a diprotic acid, as the hydrogen atom directly bonded to the central phosphorus atom is not readily ionizable. This contrasts with phosphoric acid, where all three hydrogen atoms are acidic under aqueous conditions. The monodeprotonated species, HP(O)₂(OH)⁻, is known as the phosphite ion. The IUPAC name for this species is phosphonic acid, a term often reserved for substituted derivatives where organic groups are bonded to phosphorus. For example, (CH₃)PO(OH)₂ is called methylphosphonic acid, which can form methylphosphonate esters. Both phosphorous acid and its deprotonated forms are effective reducing agents, although they are not particularly fast-reacting. They are oxidized to phosphoric acid or its salts and can reduce noble metal cations in solution to their metallic forms. Phosphorous acid has several applications. It is used to produce phosphine gas (PH₃) through thermal decomposition at approximately 180°C. Phosphine, being flammable and toxic, is inconvenient to store but can be readily generated from phosphorous acid. In agriculture, phosphorous acid is widely used as a phosphatic fertilizer. It is also employed to prepare phosphite salts, such as monopotassium phosphite and aluminum phosphonite. These salts, as well as aqueous solutions of pure phosphorous acid, are effective in controlling various microbial plant diseases, particularly those caused by Phytophthora and Pythium pathogens (oomycetes, or water molds). These pathogens are responsible for conditions like dieback/root rot and downy mildew. Treatments using trunk injections or foliar sprays containing phosphorous acid salts have shown efficacy against these infections. In Australia, antimicrobial products containing phosphorous acid salts are marketed as Yates Anti-Rot, while in the United States, aluminum salts of phosphorous acid (commonly known as Fosetyl-Al) are sold under the trade name Aliette. Phosphorous acid is also used as a chemical reagent, serving as a reducing agent that is less vigorous than hypophosphorous acid.
